defects: Changes the underlying object of study: gold's f is a genuine real-valued function of a real variable (f : ℝ → ℝ) with antitonicity/integrability stated about the continuous function itself; produced's f is a sequence (f : ℕ → ℝ), and the continuous-variable integrand is manufactured via f (Int.floor x).natAbs, i.e. a step-function extension — not the same mathematical object.

Conclusion type differs: gold concludes IntegrableOn f (Ioi N) (Bochner integrability of the original real function); produced concludes finiteness of a lower Lebesgue integral (∫⁻) of the artificially constructed step function — not equivalent to integrability of a general antitone real function.
Likely type error: ∫⁻ requires an ℝ≥0∞-valued integrand, but f (Int.floor x).natAbs has type ℝ with no ENNReal.ofReal coercion applied, so the statement as written likely does not typecheck.
Loses generality of starting point: gold has a free parameter N : ℕ for where the ray/antitonicity begins; produced hard-codes the ray to start at 1.

Antitone hypothesis differs in domain: gold's AntitoneOn f (Ici N) is a genuine continuous-domain monotonicity condition; produced's Antitone f only constrains the discrete sequence, and antitonicity of the constructed step function on the reals is not asserted or equivalent to a continuous integrability statement.

Trivializes the theorem: because the constructed integrand is constant on each unit interval [n, n+1), finiteness of its lintegral is essentially definitionally equivalent to Summable f, so the produced statement no longer captures the substantive integral-comparison-test content (relating integrability of a general antitone continuous function to summability of its samples) that the gold statement expresses.
Nonnegativity hypothesis only covers the sequence (∀ n, 0 ≤ f n) rather than the gold's pointwise nonnegativity on the whole ray (∀ t ∈ Ioi N, 0 ≤ f t) for a continuous-domain function.
